## The argument in one paragraph

Economic growth over the last two centuries created unprecedented wealth — and, along the way, climate change. The degrowth movement concludes that the way to fix the environment is to stop, or reverse, growth. This rests on a misunderstanding of what economists mean by growth and what actually drives emissions. The real problem is not the *flow* of output but the *stock of dirty capital* we have built up. Stopping growth does almost nothing about that stock — we would keep emitting far too much every year even in a perfectly stagnant economy. The only way out is to *rebuild* the capital stock as clean capital, and that is an investment problem that shrinking the economy makes harder, not easier. So the honest slogan is not degrowth but **regrowth** — and you can test the logic yourself with the interactive model below.

## Why do economies grow?

The workhorse model of growth is the Solow model. Output is produced from capital $K$, labour $L$ and a technology level $A$ via a Cobb–Douglas production function, $Y = A\,K^{\alpha}L^{1-\alpha}$, with **decreasing returns to each individual factor**. Capital has to be produced: it rises with the saved-and-invested share $s$ of output and falls as a fraction $\delta$ depreciates each year. Because investment runs into decreasing returns while depreciation is proportional to the stock, the economy converges to a **steady state** and then stops growing. Capital accumulation alone cannot sustain growth, and population growth cannot raise output *per head*. The only thing that does is **technological progress** \[Solow 1956\].

The implication for the degrowth debate is immediate: in the long run, "growth" and "innovation" are the same thing. To *permanently* stop growth you would have to stop innovation — which is neither desirable (innovation is our main tool against climate change) nor feasible. This is essentially the case Aghion and co-authors make in *The Power of Creative Destruction* \[Aghion, Antonin & Bunel 2021\]; van den Bergh \[2011\] makes the more careful version — that a deliberate GDP contraction would starve the clean investment we need — and pleads for "a-growth".

## But growth is not the problem — the capital stock is

The usual green-growth reply is that richer economies are less carbon-intensive, because people buy more low-carbon services. True, but it misses the binding constraint. Even if every extra unit of output were a zero-carbon service, the **dirty capital we already own keeps emitting** — coal plants, blast furnaces, gas boilers, petrol cars. Put it at its sharpest: *even a perfectly stagnant, zero-growth economy would still emit far too much every year.* A smaller economy full of dirty capital is still a dirty economy. The only way to cut emissions is to *replace* the dirty capital stock with clean capital — an investment problem.

## Try it yourself

Split the capital stock into **dirty** capital $K_D$ and **clean** capital $K_C$ (clean is initially less productive, weighted by $\phi<1$). Pollution is a property of the dirty part, $P = \omega\,Y\,\tfrac{K_D}{K_D+K_C}$, where $\omega$ is emissions per unit of dirty output. Technology need not be neutral either: dirty technology improves at rate $g$, while clean technology improves at $g_C = g - 1 + (A_D/A_C)^{\xi}$ — with $\xi>0$, clean enjoys a temporary growth **bonus** proportional to how far it lags the frontier, so $\phi = A_C/A_D$ converges towards 1 and the bonus melts away; with $\xi=0$ (the default) both improve at $g$ and the gap is frozen. An empirical motivation for such a clean growth premium is that clean technologies generate substantially larger **knowledge spillovers** than dirty ones — clean patents attract up to 40% more citations ([Dechezleprêtre, Martin & Mohnen 2017](https://www.lse.ac.uk/granthaminstitute/publication/knowledge-spillovers-from-clean-and-dirty-technologies-a-patent-citation-analysis-working-paper-135/)), the returns to supporting clean innovation are correspondingly higher ([Martin & Verhoeven 2023](https://cep.lse.ac.uk/_NEW/PUBLICATIONS/abstract.asp?index=10290)), and green innovation is diffusing rapidly to emerging economies ([IFC 2025](https://www.ifc.org/en/insights-reports/2025/innovation-in-green-technologies)). Each economy has its own policy sliders — how much to invest in dirty vs. clean capital, and how hard to work — so you can compare **your economy** (red — by default it runs the **green transition**, with all saving redirected to clean capital) against **business as usual** (grey, which keeps investing in dirty capital at 5%). The technology and valuation parameters below the two columns apply to both, and a toggle switches every chart between levels and period growth rates.

```{ojs}
function runModel(sd, sc, L, g, xeta, omega, phi0) {
  const alpha = 0.3, dd = 0.2, dc = 0.2, N = 25;
  let Kd = 0.1, Kc = 0.0, A = 0.75, phi = phi0;  // A = A_D; phi = A_C/A_D
  let K = Kd + phi*Kc;
  let Y = Math.pow(K, alpha) * A;   // L=1 at the common start
  let Id = 0.05*Y, Ic = 0.0;
  const out = [{t: 1, Y, poll: omega*Y*Kd/(Kd+Kc), cons: Y*(1-0.05), ratio: phi}];
  for (let t = 2; t <= N; t++) {
    const nKd = Kd*(1-dd) + Id, nKc = Kc*(1-dc) + Ic;
    Kd = nKd; Kc = nKc;
    const gc = g - 1 + Math.pow(1/phi, xeta);  // clean tech: g_C = g - 1 + (A_D/A_C)^xi
    A = A*(1+g);                           // dirty technology grows at g
    phi = phi*(1+gc)/(1+g);                // xi > 0: the gap closes over time
    K = Kd + phi*Kc;
    Y = Math.pow(K, alpha) * Math.pow(L, 1-alpha) * A;
    Id = sd*Y; Ic = sc*Y;
    out.push({t, Y, poll: omega*Y*Kd/(Kd+Kc), cons: Y*(1-sd-sc), ratio: phi});
  }
  return out;
}

series = {
  const addNet = d => ({...d, netY: d.Y - tau*d.poll});
  const you = runModel(sd, sc, Lval, g, xeta, omega, phi).map(d => ({...addNet(d), who: "Your economy"}));
  const bau = runModel(sdb, scb, Lb, g, xeta, omega, phi).map(d => ({...addNet(d), who: "Business as usual"}));
  return bau.concat(you);
}

col = ({legend: true, domain: ["Business as usual", "Your economy"], range: ["#5b6773", "#A5332B"]})

function chart(y, label) {
  const data = rates
    ? series.map(d => {
        const prev = series.find(p => p.who === d.who && p.t === d.t - 1);
        const ok = prev && prev[y] > 0 && Number.isFinite(d[y]);
        return {...d, val: ok ? (d[y]/prev[y] - 1)*100 : NaN};
      }).filter(d => Number.isFinite(d.val))
    : series.map(d => ({...d, val: d[y]}));
  return Plot.plot({
    height: 240, marginLeft: 55, marginBottom: 35,
    x: {label: "Period →"},
    y: {label: rates ? label + " — growth, %/period" : label, grid: true, zero: true},
    color: col,
    marks: [ Plot.line(data, {x: "t", y: "val", stroke: "who", strokeWidth: 2.6}) ]
  });
}
```

A few experiments to try. **Degrowth alone:** leave clean savings at zero and pull *Work / labour* down — pollution barely moves, because the dirty capital is still running. **The transition:** set dirty savings to zero and clean savings to 5% — emissions fall as the dirty stock depreciates away. **Invest more:** push clean savings to 10% — emissions fall faster *and* output ends up higher. **Degrowth + transition:** now also cut *Work / labour* — you get the emissions cut, but it's the most painful path for consumption, because you're rebuilding the capital stock with a smaller surplus. **Catch-up:** push $\xi$ above zero — clean technology grows faster than dirty *for a while*, with a bonus that shrinks as it closes the gap, so $\phi$ climbs towards 1 and the transition gets ever cheaper; at $\xi=0$ the productivity gap is frozen and lock-in persists.

## Does the GDP critique rescue degrowth?

A standard objection at this point: *"GDP is a poor measure of wellbeing, so maximising it is the wrong objective in the first place."* We agree with the premise — and the model already contains the fix. Assign a monetary value $\tau$ to each unit of emissions and compute **net GDP**,

$$Y^{net} = Y - \tau \cdot P,$$

which is precisely what the *Net GDP* tab above shows (move the $\tau$ slider to make the environmental damage weigh as heavily as you like). Two things follow.

First, **re-valuing output does not change the dynamics**. Net GDP is a different way of *scoring* the paths, but the paths themselves — how capital accumulates, what pollutes — are untouched. The degrowth path (work less, keep the dirty investment pattern) is a one-off cut to the *level* of output; the growth *rate* is still set by technical progress $g$. Push $\tau$ as high as you like: working less still barely dents pollution, because the dirty capital stock is still there and still running. Indeed, as long as $g>0$ — even if fewer hours also slowed innovation somewhat — output, and with it emissions, keeps growing without bound on the degrowth path. A level shift is asymptotically irrelevant against exponential growth.

Second, and more interestingly: **taking net GDP seriously leads to green growth, not degrowth**. With a high $\tau$, the path that maximises net GDP is not the one that works less — it is the one that redirects investment from dirty to clean capital, because that is what removes the $\tau\cdot P$ penalty while keeping output. If society actually *priced* emissions at $\tau$, firms would make exactly that reallocation on their own — the emissions price is the transition policy. The GDP critique, followed to its logical end, is an argument for pricing carbon and rebuilding the capital stock — not for shrinking the economy.

One honest concession: during a *slow* transition, a temporary reduction in output does shave some cumulative emissions while the clean stock builds up — that is why the "degrowth + transition" path sits slightly below "transition alone" on pollution, at a real consumption cost. So the precise statement is: the transition is *necessary*; degrowth is *neither necessary nor sufficient* — at best a costly way to buy a little carbon-budget headroom.

## Degrowth or regrowth?

The binding constraint on emissions is the **stock of dirty capital**, not the **flow of GDP**. Stopping growth leaves that stock in place and keeps the emissions coming. The only exit is to invest in clean capital and let the dirty capital retire — a process that is easier the more output you have to invest, and hardest if you are deliberately shrinking. This is the directed-technical-change logic of Acemoglu, Aghion, Bursztyn & Hémous \[2012\] in capital-accumulation form, and a two-capital cousin of the Green Solow model \[Brock & Taylor 2010\]. So the choice is badly framed: we do not face *degrowth vs. catastrophe* but **rebuild vs. catastrophe** — and rebuilding is an investment programme that growth pays for.
